design_detail: Double-blind, within-person, placebo-controlled laboratory study in 8 adults with DSM-IV cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse who were already using both drugs together, on an inpatient unit in New Haven, Connecticut (Yale Psychiatric Institute or the Connecticut Mental Health Center). Each person attended three 480-minute sessions in random order, at least 2 days apart: four doses of intranasal cocaine with oral alcohol, the same cocaine with a placebo drink, or a placebo powder with the same alcohol. Heart rate, blood pressure, ratings of drug effects and blood levels of cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol were followed for 8 hours. Read in full from the PDF (Biol Psychiatry 1998;44:250-259); Table 1 and the heart-rate figure with its legend were checked on rendered pages. Figures 2 to 4 are images: their values were not used except the areas under the curve printed in the legend of Figure 1.
can_establish: Whether, in these 8 people under these conditions, adding alcohol to repeated intranasal cocaine changed heart rate, blood pressure, ratings of high and well-being, and the blood levels of cocaine and its alcohol-linked metabolite cocaethylene, compared with each drug alone.
cannot_establish: Anything about heart attacks, rhythm disturbances or other harm (none was measured); whether the combination leads people to take more (no self-administration or choice procedure); effects of smoked or injected cocaine, of other doses or sequences of dosing, or of the combination in people with other drinking patterns; whether the combination adds more than the sum of its parts (no test of additivity); blood-pressure effects, which this sample could not detect.

sample.recruitment: Non-treatment-seeking volunteers recruited by word of mouth or newspaper advertisement and paid for taking part (Methods and Materials > Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Actively using cocaine and alcohol together at entry, with cocaine as the preferred drug; DSM-IV cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse; full psychiatric and medical evaluation; one person also met criteria for cannabis abuse and no other substance use or psychiatric disorder was present. Participants were told to abstain from drugs and alcohol for 3 days before admission, had a urine drug screen and breathalyzer on admission, and were watched for alcohol withdrawal for 2 days (Subjects; Procedures).
sample.demographics: Mean age 33 years (SE 4); 4 men and 4 women; 7 African-American and 1 Caucasian. Printed usual intake: cocaine about 5 g a week (SE 7) by the smoked route and alcohol 14 standard drinks a week (SE 50), figures whose spread is implausible as printed (reporting issue 1).
sample.attrition: Not reported; every analysis appears to include all 8 people, but completion of all three sessions is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Eight paid volunteers who already used both drugs together, chosen on purpose so that nobody met a new combination (Discussion, p. 257). They usually smoked cocaine but received it intranasally, so results come from people with tolerance to both drugs and may not carry over to people who use the drugs less often or by other routes; the authors say the intranasal route probably understates effects seen with smoked or injected cocaine.

exposure.measurement: Study-administered drugs, dosed by lean body weight; blood concentrations of cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol measured by liquid and gas chromatography with reproducibility below 5%.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: cocaine hydrochloride powder 1 mg/kg intranasally at 0, 30, 60 and 90 minutes; oral alcohol 1 g/kg after the first cocaine dose and 120 mg/kg at 60 minutes, calculated to hold plasma alcohol near 100 mg/dL during the cocaine doses; the third session used lactose in place of cocaine and the second a placebo drink in place of alcohol (Study Design). Plasma alcohol 30 minutes after the second drink averaged 99 mg/dL (SE 7) with cocaine and 118 (SE 10) without.
exposure.polysubstance: One participant also met cannabis abuse criteria; no urine results on admission are reported beyond the screen having been done; other substances were not tested during sessions.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Told to abstain for 3 days before admission and checked by urine screen and breathalyzer; watched for withdrawal for 2 days.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant received all three conditions (cocaine with alcohol; cocaine with placebo alcohol; placebo cocaine with alcohol) in random order, double-blind, sessions at least 2 days apart. There was no session with placebo for both drugs, so each single-drug condition is compared with the combination, not with nothing.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to within-person contrasts, but tolerance, usual dose and craving differ between people and were not analysed as moderators; the authors raise whether people who use both drugs differ from people who use cocaine alone as an open question.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Everyone already used both drugs together; one also met cannabis abuse criteria; no comparison group of people who use cocaine only.

outcomes.instruments: Heart rate and blood pressure by automated monitor (Hewlett-Packard 43200A) with cardiac rhythm monitoring until 3 hours after the last cocaine dose; 100-mm visual analogue scales for any high, rush, sleepy, paranoid, sad or depressed, crash, desire for cocaine and feel good; a five-anchor rating of the quality of the cocaine high; clinician-rated analogue scales; plasma cocaine and cocaethylene by reverse-phase liquid chromatography; plasma alcohol by gas chromatography.
outcomes.validity_norms: Assays cite earlier validation; the analogue scales are standard in laboratory work. Clinician ratings were collected to confirm drug effects but are not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: For each measure, the area under the curve (AUC) over the session, compared between the combination and each single drug by planned comparisons; pharmacokinetic values (peak, half-life, AUC) from a multiple-dose one-compartment model compared by paired t test.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: one set of planned one-tailed comparisons for each of 15 measures (heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure, eight ratings, plasma cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol), justified by directional hypotheses taken from the authors' earlier study (Data Analysis, p. 252).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Described as double-blind; how the alcohol and cocaine placebos were masked, and whether participants could tell the conditions apart, is not described. Participants knew the three possible conditions, and both intranasal cocaine and 1 g/kg of alcohol are noticeable in people who take them regularly.

analysis.effect_sizes: Heart rate (repeated-measures ANOVA on AUC; planned comparisons, one-tailed): combination higher than cocaine alone, p = .002, and than alcohol alone, p = .002. Printed heart-rate AUCs (mean, SEM; beats per minute x minutes, 0 to 480 min): combination 40,289 (940), cocaine 35,658 (647), alcohol 34,778 (933); editors' calculation (AUC / 480): mean 83.9, 74.3 and 72.5 beats per minute, a difference of 9.7 against cocaine alone and 11.5 against alcohol alone. Blood pressure: no significant difference between the combination and cocaine alone; combination higher than alcohol alone for systolic (p = .008) and diastolic (p = .003) pressure. Ratings: feel good higher with the combination than with cocaine alone, p = .04; any high p = .09 (not significant); the cocaine-high rating did not differ from cocaine alone and was higher than with alcohol alone, p = .002; rush, sleepy, paranoid, crash, sad or depressed and desire for cocaine showed no significant differences. Cocaine: peak 893 ng/mL (SEM 114) with alcohol against 754 (114); AUC 153,562 (19,489) against 135,371 (19,892) ng x min/mL, printed as about 15% greater, p = .035; half-life 85 (3.2) against 83 (2.9) minutes. Cocaethylene (only in the combination): half-life 156 (15.3) minutes, longer than cocaine, p = .001; peak 114 ng/mL (18) at 180 minutes, about 22% of the cocaine level then; AUC 31,050 (4,706), a ratio to cocaine AUC of 0.20 (0.01); concentration ratio about 0.13 at 120 minutes (time of peak heart rate and feel good) and 0.40 at 360 minutes. Alcohol levels were lower with cocaine than without, p = .008 (data not shown).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration (1998). Directional hypotheses are stated from the authors' earlier single-dose study, with one planned comparison per measure and one-tailed testing at .05 (Data Analysis, p. 252).
analysis.selective_reporting: Six rating measures are reported only as 'no statistically significant findings', the alcohol comparison as 'data not shown', clinician ratings not at all, and heart rate appears as means only in a figure, with AUCs in its legend; effect sizes and intervals are never given.
analysis.power: Not discussed; 8 people, and a one-tailed p of .035 to .09 on the ratings and cocaine AUC.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 8 people who already used both drugs, four intranasal cocaine doses taken with oral alcohol produced a higher heart rate over 8 hours than the same cocaine with a placebo drink (mean about 84 against 74 beats per minute, editors' calculation) or the same alcohol with placebo cocaine (about 72), a roughly 13% larger cocaine exposure (p = .035, one-tailed), cocaethylene with a half-life nearly twice that of cocaine, and higher ratings of feeling good than cocaine alone (p = .04, one-tailed), without a significant rise in ratings of any high (p = .09) or in blood pressure over cocaine alone.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract say the combination is more potent and potentially more toxic and produced greater euphoria; the abstract concludes that stronger psychological effects may encourage people to take larger amounts and so run a higher risk of toxicity; the discussion says the findings point to an increased risk of organ ischaemia, infarction and arrhythmia and that combined use is a likely factor in adverse events now attributed to cocaine alone, and credits cocaethylene with a role in the heart-rate effect.

timeline.event: Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat (Life Sciences): single doses of cocaine after alcohol, as described by Pennings et al. (2002; not read): cocaethylene formed, plasma cocaine higher, heart-rate rises additive

Farre et al. (J Pharmacol Exp Ther) and McCance-Katz et al. (Psychopharmacology), single-dose studies as described by Pennings et al. (2002; not read): cocaethylene formed, plasma cocaine up to 30% higher with alcohol, greater-than-additive or additive heart-rate rises

Perez-Reyes (Life Sciences), as described by Pennings et al. (2002; not read): when cocaine was taken 30 minutes before alcohol, plasma cocaine and heart rate did not rise above the single-drug levels
Signs et al. (as described by Pennings et al.; not read): over 1,000 emergency-room toxicology screens showed no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one

Pennings et al. review (Addiction): lists this study among 14 prospective studies and gives its heart-rate result as greater than additive and its dosing as alcohol first, neither of which this paper states

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the heart-rate, blood-cocaine and cocaethylene findings agrees with earlier single-dose laboratory studies as described in the one review read; the heart-rate result is reported there to depend on dosing order, and retrospective emergency-room data do not show a clear excess of cardiovascular problems. This multiple-dose design has no replication among the sources read; the euphoria finding is the weakest part.

funding.funder: Supported in part by US Public Health Service grants K20-DA00216 and R29-DA09573 (McCance-Katz), K02-DA00112 (Kosten), P50-DA04060 and M01-RR00125, and by the Connecticut Department of Mental Health (Acknowledgments, p. 258).
funding.affiliations_note: Yale Psychiatric Institute and the General Clinical Research Center; Connecticut Mental Health Center; Departments of Psychiatry and Laboratory Medicine, Yale University School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized, double-blind crossover study with a session of placebo for both drugs, two-tailed tests with intervals, heart rhythm and blood-pressure outcomes, both orders of dosing, smoked as well as intranasal cocaine, measured cocaethylene kinetics, and a self-administration or choice procedure to test whether the combination changes how much is taken.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the three sessions)
domains.note: Order was random but how it was generated and concealed is not described, and no order or period effect is reported.
At least 2 days between sessions, longer than the half-lives measured; heart rate had not returned to baseline by 8 hours after the combination, and no check for carryover is reported.

Double-blind in form, but 1 g/kg of alcohol and intranasal cocaine are noticeable in people who take them regularly, participants knew the three possible conditions and the masking of the placebos is not described; the ratings that carry the euphoria finding are self-rated.
All 8 people appear in every analysis; completion is not stated explicitly.
Heart rate, blood pressure and drug concentrations are instrument-measured; the euphoria and well-being ratings are self-rated, and the clinician ratings are not reported.
No registration; 15 measures tested one-tailed without correction; several results given only as 'not significant' or 'data not shown'; no intervals or effect sizes.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A within-person, randomized-order, double-blind comparison with objective drug levels is a sound way to study this pair, and the heart-rate and drug-level findings are large relative to their printed spread. The overall judgment is set by the unmaskable alcohol condition, by 8 participants, by one-tailed uncorrected tests and by reporting that gives p values but few numbers. The source may be cited for what happened in these sessions: a higher heart rate and a somewhat higher cocaine exposure with the combination, cocaethylene formed only with the combination and cleared more slowly than cocaine, and no detectable blood-pressure difference from cocaine alone. It may not be cited for greater euphoria beyond the single feel-good rating, for toxicity, for additivity, for risk of heart events, or for smoked or injected cocaine.

key_findings.finding: Eight volunteers (4 men and 4 women, mean age 33 years, SE 4; 7 African-American and 1 Caucasian), non-treatment-seeking, recruited by word of mouth or newspaper advertisement and paid; actively using cocaine and alcohol together at entry with cocaine as the preferred drug; DSM-IV cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse; one also met cannabis abuse criteria. Printed usual intake: cocaine about 5 g a week (SE 7) by smoking; alcohol 14 standard drinks a week (SE 50).

Inpatient stay for the whole study; told to abstain from drugs and alcohol for 3 days before admission; urine drug screen and breathalyzer on admission; watched for alcohol withdrawal for the first 2 days.

Double-blind, within-person, three 480-minute sessions in random order, no more often than every 2 days: four doses of intranasal cocaine hydrochloride (1 mg/kg every 30 minutes) with oral alcohol (1 g/kg after the first cocaine dose and 120 mg/kg at 60 minutes, calculated to hold plasma alcohol near 100 mg/dL); the same cocaine with placebo alcohol; lactose in place of cocaine with the same alcohol. Participants knew the three possible conditions. Doses were calculated from lean body weight.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Study Design, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blood sampling and monitoring at 16 time points between -15 and 480 minutes; heart rate and blood pressure by automated monitor; cardiac rhythm monitoring for 3 hours after the last cocaine dose; analogue scales for any high, rush, sleepy, paranoid, sad or depressed, crash, desire for cocaine and feel good; a five-anchor quality-of-high scale; clinician-rated scales.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Cocaine Study Drug Administration Sessions, 1st paragraph (starts p. 251)

key_findings.finding: Analysis: AUC of each measure over the session in a repeated-measures ANOVA, then planned comparisons of the combination with each drug alone; only one set of comparisons per measure because the authors had directional hypotheses from earlier work; every test with p below .05 one-tailed counted as significant; pharmacokinetic parameters (one-compartment model) compared by paired t test.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Pharmacokinetics Analyses, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Heart rate was higher with the combination than with cocaine alone (p = .002) or alcohol alone (p = .002) after each dose of study drug. Printed AUCs in the Figure 1 legend: combination 40,289 (SEM 940), cocaine 35,658 (647), alcohol 34,778 (933); editors' calculation (AUC / 480 minutes): mean 83.9, 74.3 and 72.5 beats per minute.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 252); Figure 1 and its legend (p. 253)
key_findings.note: Means over time appear only in the figure, an image; no heart-rate values are given in the text.

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure: both cocaine conditions raised systolic and diastolic pressure; no significant difference between the combination and cocaine alone; the combination was higher than alcohol alone for systolic (p = .008) and diastolic (p = .003) pressure.

Any high was greater with the combination than with cocaine alone, approaching significance (p = .09); the cocaine-high rating did not differ from cocaine alone and was higher than with alcohol alone (p = .002); feel good was higher than with cocaine alone (p = .04), peaking at 120 minutes. Cocaine alone gave no rise in feel good over the session.
Rush, sleepy, paranoid, crash, sad or depressed, and desire for cocaine: no statistically significant findings (no values given).

Peak cocaine concentration 893 ng/mL (SEM 114) at 113 minutes with alcohol and 754 (114) at 116 minutes without; AUC 153,562 (19,489) against 135,371 (19,892) ng x min/mL, described as about 15% greater with alcohol (p = .035); cocaine half-life 85 (3.2) and 83 (2.9) minutes.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed means: AUC ratio 1.134 and peak ratio 1.184; the peak difference is not tested.

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene appeared only with the combination; half-life 156 (SEM 15.3) minutes, longer than cocaine (p = .001); peak 114 ng/mL (18) at 180 minutes, about 22% of the cocaine concentration then; concentration ratio to cocaine about 0.13 at 120 minutes, rising to 0.40 at 360 minutes; AUC 31,050 (4,706) ng x min/mL, a ratio of 0.20 (0.01) to the cocaine AUC.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (continued, p. 253); Table 1 (p. 255); Discussion, 4th paragraph (pp. 256-257)

key_findings.finding: Plasma alcohol was higher with alcohol alone than with the combination (p = .008; data not shown); 30 minutes after the second alcohol dose it averaged 99 mg/dL (SE 7) with cocaine and 118 (10) without. The authors suggest swallowed cocaine reduces alcohol absorption through gastric vasoconstriction.

Heart rate remained above baseline at 8 hours after the combination; the authors suggest cocaethylene, whose ratio to cocaine reached 0.40 late in the session, may matter more for heart effects than for the early high, and that it 'probably contributes minimally' to the initial high; no test separates cocaethylene from the rise in cocaine.

Stated limits: intranasal route (smoked or injected cocaine may give larger effects); participants were chosen because they already used both drugs; whether people who use both drugs differ in vulnerability, or the combination is more toxic to the brain, is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Usual intake is printed as 14 standard drinks a week with a standard error of 50, and cocaine as 5 g a week with a standard error of 7: for 8 people these spreads are far larger than the means (a standard error of 50 implies a standard deviation near 140 drinks a week), so a symbol or figure is misprinted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Participants' tolerance to each drug cannot be judged from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and title say the combination produced greater euphoria and is more potent, but any high rose only to p = .09 and the cocaine-high rating did not differ from cocaine alone; only feel good differed (p = .04, one-tailed, which is about .08 two-tailed by the editors' calculation of doubling).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the study for a higher feel-good rating, not for a general increase in euphoria.

reporting_issues.issue: All tests are one-tailed at .05, justified by hypotheses taken from the authors' earlier study, with no correction across 15 measures; the cocaine AUC (p = .035) and feel-good (p = .04) results would not be significant at .05 two-tailed (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The heart-rate result (p = .002) survives; the cocaine-exposure and feel-good results are fragile.

reporting_issues.issue: Cocaine AUC is described as about 15% greater with alcohol, but the printed means give 13.4% (153,562 against 135,371); the peak values have the same printed standard error (114) and the peak difference is untested; heart-rate means are shown only in a figure, with no table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote exposure as roughly 13% to 15% higher; do not quote a heart-rate difference in beats per minute except as the editors' calculation from the AUCs.

reporting_issues.issue: Clinician-rated analogue scales were collected as a method of 'observing and confirming drug effects' but their results are absent; six rating items and the alcohol-level comparison are reported without values.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unreported measures cannot be weighed; negative findings are known only as 'not significant' in 8 people.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusions that stronger psychological effects will lead people to take more and that toxicity will follow, and the discussion's statement that the findings point to an increased risk of ischaemia, infarction and arrhythmia, go beyond what was measured: there was no self-administration procedure and no heart events or rhythm findings are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the study for heart rate and drug levels, not for clinical harm or for a change in how much is taken.

reporting_issues.issue: Doses were fixed by body weight and given intranasally on a fixed schedule to people who usually smoked cocaine, and the second alcohol dose was timed to hold a target blood level; the paper presents this as closer to street practice than single-dose studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat the doses and timing as study conditions, not as what happens outside the laboratory.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 250-259 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/McCanceKatz_1998_CocaineAlcoholMultipleDose.pdf), full text including the reference list; Table 1 and Figure 1 (with its legend) checked on rendered pages 253 and 255; Figures 2 to 4 are images and no values were read from them.
